t: Idris I, a great-grandson of Hasan ibn Ali, fled the Abbasids after the Battle of Fakhkh and was made imam by the Awraba Berbers of Volubilis in 788.
Idris II moved his seat to Fez in 809 and welcomed Arab settlers from Córdoba in 818 and from Aghlabid Tunisia in 824, giving the city its Arab character.
After Idris II's death in 828 the realm was divided among his sons; the Idrisids lost Fez for good in 927 and were removed from power by the Umayyads of Córdoba in 974.
dyk: Idris I left no male heir when an Abbasid agent poisoned him in 791, but his wife Lalla Kanza bore his only son shortly after his death; the boy, Idris II, was proclaimed imam by the Awraba at the age of eleven.
ev: Idris ibn Abdallah, fleeing the Abbasids after the Battle of Fakhkh, settles at Volubilis, where the Awraba Berbers make him their imam.
Idris I is poisoned by an Abbasid agent; his posthumous son Idris II is brought up under the regency of the freedman Rashid.
Idris II has the Awraba leader Ishak killed and moves his seat from Walili to Fez, founding the settlement of al-'Aliya.
Idris II dies; the state reaches from western Algeria to the Sous, and his son Muhammad divides it among seven brothers.
Ali ibn Muhammad and Yahya I rule in stability; the al-Qarawiyyin and al-Andalusiyyin mosques are founded in Fez.
The Sufri Kharijite tribes of Madyuna, Ghayata and Miknasa defeat Ali ibn Umar and occupy Fez until Yahya III retakes it.
Musa ibn Abul 'Afiya of the Miknasa captures and kills Hassan I al-Hajam: the Idrisids never again hold Fez.
The Umayyad general Ghalib expels the Idrisids from their lands and takes al-Hasan and other Idrisids as hostages to Córdoba.

f.capital: Volubilis (Walili), then Fez (al-'Aliya, from 809); Hajar an-Nasr after 927
f.founder: Idris I (Idris ibn Abdallah), made imam by the Awraba Berbers of Volubilis in 788
f.predecessor: The Berber tribes and principalities of Morocco, independent of the caliphs since the Kharijite revolts of 739–40; the Awraba of Volubilis
f.successor: The Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba in northern Morocco (974); then the Zenata Maghrawa and Banu Ifran
